title: An open home
hookLine: Abraham's tent, lived: a spare chair at the table
tomorrow: an old father told his son to turn his bookcases into what?

lines: THE SAME AFTERNOON, FROM THE FRONT.
cards: The smell of something in the oven does half the welcoming before anyone says hello. Remember Sarah, laughing at the tent door? Here's the same afternoon from the front of the tent.
It's the heat of the day. Abraham sits at the entrance and sees three strangers on the road. And Genesis says "he ran to meet them from the tent door."
An old man, in the heat, running.

teach.b: Look at the details Genesis keeps, and how many of them you could touch or taste. Water for dusty feet: "Let now a little water be fetched, and wash your feet." Shade: rest under the tree.
Bread: Abraham hurries into the tent to ask Sarah for cakes. A tender calf, butter and milk. He offers a morsel of bread and serves a feast.

teach.h: A TENT OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.
teach.b: Avot de-Rabbi Natan adds a detail Genesis doesn't have: Abraham's tent had openings on every side, so no traveler had to hunt for the door.

teach.h: LET YOUR HOUSE BE OPEN WIDE.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot turns it into a rule for every home: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household. The name for this is hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests. Notice the order.
It's physical first: a seat, water, something warm. The talk comes after.

So a spare chair at the table is the modern tent flap. It says, before anyone speaks, there's room for you. Something to tell a friend tonight: Abraham promised a bite of bread and then brought out a feast.

how: Hachnasat orchim is a mitzvah Jews practice by inviting guests to Shabbat and holiday meals, hosting travelers and newcomers, and at the Passover seder opening with 'let all who are hungry come and eat'.

o: a home that welcomes guests, with room to spare
a house with no locks on any of its doors
a family that moves to a new town often

p: no one hunts for the door
let your house be open wide

s: Abraham waited for the strangers to ask for help
he ran to meet them from the tent door.
the tent open on every side comes from Avot de-Rabbi Natan, not Genesis
Genesis gives the water, shade and bread; the open sides are a later teaching.
hospitality in this tradition means putting on a fancy meal
Abraham's welcome starts with water, shade and a seat; the feast came after.

games.q: a new hire at your work eats lunch alone every day. there's an empty seat at your table. what would Abraham's tent do?
o: wave him over before he has to ask.
wait until he asks if he can join.
invite him once you know him better.
games.why: Abraham ran to meet them. the welcome comes first, before anyone knows anyone.

practice: If there's something to drink near you, water or tea, hold it and smell it first, then take one slow sip, the way a guest would after a long road. Notice how it lands.
Then bring to mind one person who'd be glad to be offered exactly this, in a spare chair at your table.

wordCard.voice: An open home: hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests. Water, shade, bread, and a way in on every side.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing in guests, the mitzvah of hospitality.

carryVoice: For the road: a spare chair, and water offered before the questions. Day twelve, door open.
